title: Island Perimeter
problemStatement: You are given a grid of 0's (water) and 1's (land) forming exactly one island (no lakes, one connected component, no diagonal connections). Return the perimeter of the island.
approachSteps: Every land cell contributes up to 4 units of perimeter (its four edges) — but any edge it SHARES with a neighboring land cell is an internal edge, not part of the island's outer boundary.
For each land cell, start by adding 4 to the running perimeter total.

Then check its up neighbor and its left neighbor (only these two, to avoid double-counting each shared edge from both sides): if either is also land, subtract 2 from the total — 1 for this cell's edge that's no longer exposed, and 1 for the neighbor's matching edge.
Summing this across every land cell in the grid gives the total perimeter directly, with no separate boundary-tracing step needed.

bruteForce.approach: There isn't a meaningfully different brute force — checking each land cell's neighbors is already the natural, optimal approach; the only variation is which neighbors you check to avoid double-counting shared edges.

optimalApproach: For every land cell, add 4 to the perimeter, then subtract 2 for each land neighbor found by checking only up and left (each shared edge detected exactly once this way).
timeComplexity: O(rows * cols) — every cell is visited once.
followUps: Why is checking only up and left (not all 4 directions) enough to correctly avoid double-counting shared edges?
How would you adapt this if the grid could contain multiple islands and you needed the perimeter of the LARGEST one?

title: Spiral Matrix
problemStatement: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (starting top-left, going right, then down, then left, then up, shrinking inward).
approachSteps: The spiral traces the outer boundary of a shrinking rectangle repeatedly — track that rectangle explicitly with four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) instead of trying to compute a direction/turn logic per cell.
Traverse across the top row (left to right), then increment top (that row is now 'consumed').
Traverse down the right column (top to bottom), then decrement right.
If there are still rows left (top <= bottom), traverse across the bottom row (right to left), then decrement bottom.
If there are still columns left (left <= right), traverse up the left column (bottom to top), then increment left.
Repeat this four-sided sweep while top <= bottom and left <= right — the two 'if' guards on the second half of each lap prevent re-visiting cells on matrices that aren't square.

bruteForce.approach: Simulate a walker with a direction vector, turning 90 degrees clockwise whenever the next cell is out of bounds or already visited (tracked in a separate visited grid).
bruteForce.spaceComplexity: O(rows * cols) for the visited grid

optimalApproach: Shrink four explicit boundaries (top/bottom/left/right) inward one full lap at a time, with guards to avoid re-traversing a row or column that's already been fully consumed.
timeComplexity: O(rows * cols) — every cell is visited exactly once.
spaceComplexity: O(1) extra (excluding the output array) — no visited grid needed, unlike the direction-vector simulation.
followUps: Why are the bottom-row and left-column traversals guarded with 'if top <= bottom' / 'if left <= right' but the top-row and right-column ones aren't?
How would you generate a spiral matrix (the reverse problem: fill an n x n grid with 1..n^2 in spiral order) using the same boundary-shrinking idea?

title: Rotate Image
problemStatement: You are given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise, in-place (you must modify the input matrix directly, without allocating another matrix).
approachSteps: A 90-degree clockwise rotation can be decomposed into two simpler, well-known in-place operations instead of computing new coordinates directly cell by cell.
Step 1 — transpose the matrix: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for every pair above the diagonal, turning rows into columns.
Step 2 — reverse each row of the transposed matrix left-to-right.

The combination of 'transpose, then reverse each row' is mathematically equivalent to a 90-degree clockwise rotation — worth verifying by hand on a small 3x3 example to build confidence in why it works.

bruteForce.approach: Allocate a new n x n matrix, and for each cell (i, j) in the original, place its value at (j, n-1-i) in the new matrix, then copy the new matrix back over the original.

optimalApproach: Transpose the matrix in-place (swap across the diagonal), then reverse each row in-place — two simple, well-understood operations replacing a direct coordinate-mapping formula.
timeComplexity: O(n^2) — every cell is touched a constant number of times across the transpose and reverse steps.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — modifies the input matrix directly, no second matrix allocated.
followUps: How would you rotate 90 degrees COUNTERclockwise instead — does the same transpose-then-reverse trick apply with a different reverse direction?
Derive the direct coordinate formula (without transpose+reverse) for where matrix[i][j] ends up after a clockwise rotation, and confirm it matches this two-step approach.
